ety.text: From Middle English som, sum, from Old English sum (“some, a certain one”), from Proto-West Germanic *sum, from Proto-Germanic *sumaz (“some, a certain one”), from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“one, whole”). Cognate Scots sum, some (“some”), North Frisian som, sam, säm (“some”), West Frisian sommige, somlike (“some”), dialectal Dutch som, saom (“some”), standard Dutch sommige (“some”), Low German somige (“some”), German dialectal summige (“some”), Danish somme (“some”), Swedish somlig (“some”), Norwegian sum, som (“some”), Icelandic sumur (“some”), Gothic 𐍃𐌿𐌼𐍃 (sums, “one, someone”).

senses.d: A certain number (multiple but not all).
ex: Some enjoy spicy food, others prefer it milder.

senses.d: An indefinite quantity.
ex: Can I have some of them?

senses.d: An indefinite amount; a part. Used mostly with abstract and nonliving objects.
ex: Please give me some of the cake.
Everyone is wrong some of the time.

senses.d: Someone, a certain person.
ex: Euery counseller extolleth counsell; but there is some that counselleth for himselfe.

senses.d: A nonzero, unspecified proportion of (a bounded set of countable things): at least two.
ex: Near-synonym: any
Some people like camping.

senses.d: A nonzero, unspecified quantity or number of (an unbounded set of countable things).
ex: Near-synonym: any
Would you like some grapes?

senses.d: An unspecified amount of (something uncountable).
ex: Near-synonym: any
Would you like some water?

senses.d: A certain, an unspecified or unknown.
ex: I've just met some guy who said he knew you.
The sequence S converges to zero for some initial value v.

senses.d: A considerable quantity or number of.
ex: He had edited the paper for some years.
He stopped working some time ago.

senses.d: Approximately, about (with a number).
ex: She has worked at the company for some thirty years now. (31 and two months, to be exact.)
There were only some three or four cars in the lot at the time.

senses.d: Emphasizing a number.
ex: She has worked at the company for some five years now! How remarkable!

senses.d: A remarkable.
ex: He is some acrobat!
That was some speech you gave!

senses.d: Of a measurement: approximately, roughly.
ex: I guess he must have weighed some 90 kilos.
Some 30,000 spectators witnessed the feat.

senses.d: To a certain extent, or for a certain period.
ex: They walked some and talked some.

senses.d: Somewhat, a little.
ex: It looked some like Muriel, but not enough to be sure by any manner of means.

Can you get me someone more knowledgeable?

senses.d: A partially specified but unnamed person.
ex: Do you need a gift for that special someone?

senses.d: An important person.
ex: He thinks he has become someone.

senses.d: Some unspecified person.

senses.d: Synonym of someone; an important person.
ex: He could have been somebody!

senses.d: Any person.
ex: So there, I know, was somebody or a combination of somebodys who did not know what the heck they were doing or dealing with.

senses.d: A recognised or important person, a celebrity.
ex: I'm tired of being a nobody – I want to be a somebody.

From Middle English somþyng, some-thing, som thing, sum thinge, sum þinge, from Old English sum þing (literally “some thing”), equivalent to some + thing. Compare Old English āwiht (“something”, literally “some thing, any thing”), Swedish någonting (“something”, literally “some thing, any thing”).

senses.d: An uncertain or unspecified thing; one thing.
ex: I must have forgotten to pack something, but I can't think what.
I have something for you in my bag.

senses.d: A quality to a moderate degree.
ex: The performance was something of a disappointment.
That child is something of a genius.

senses.d: A talent or quality that is difficult to specify.
ex: She has a certain something.

senses.d: Somebody who or something that is superlative or notable in some way.
ex: He's really something! I've never heard such a great voice.
She's quite something. I can't believe she would do such a mean thing.

senses.d: Having a characteristic that the speaker cannot specify.
ex: She was so something that she cried all the way home.
"Very poetic." They came to a halt before the outer door. "It's very something," Rusty said wistfully. "How do you do it?"

senses.d: Somewhat; to a degree.
ex: The baby looks something like his father.

Angelo. Yet giue leaue (my Lord,)
That we may bring you something on the way

senses.d: Used to adverbialise a following adjective
ex: I miss them something terrible/rotten. (I miss them terribly)
You can't thrash when you have rheumatic fever – though you want to something awful, Mrs. White says.

senses.d: Designates an action whose name is forgotten by, unknown or unimportant to the user, e.g. from words of a song.
An object whose nature is yet to be defined.
An object whose name is forgotten by, unknown or unimportant to the user, e.g., from words of a song. Also used to refer to an object earlier indefinitely referred to as 'something' (pronoun sense).
ex: What was the something the pilot saw, the something worth killing for?

ety.text: From some + where.

senses.d: In an uncertain or unspecified location.
ex: I must have left my glasses somewhere.
I've hidden candy somewhere in this room.

senses.d: To an uncertain or unspecified location.
ex: He plans to go somewhere warm for his vacation.
I have to go somewhere at lunch. Can I meet you at 2?

senses.d: At some unspecified point.
ex: I don't remember the exact number, but it was somewhere between 200 and 300.

senses.d: Unspecified or unknown (unlocated) place or location.
ex: A courting owl hoots in the somewheres of the night and another answers its call further off.
[…] and it transports the person to a somewhere, a somewhere that the music dictates.

senses.d: A person with strong cultural or social ties that are exclusive to a specific place.

From Middle English sumtymes, somtymes, som tymes, equivalent to sometime + -s (adverbial suffix). Compare West Frisian somstiden (“sometimes”), Dutch somtijds, somwijlen (“sometimes”).

senses.d: On some occasions, over some periods, or in certain circumstances, but not always.
ex: Sometimes I sit and think, but mostly I just sit.
In 16th and 17th century Britain, for example, women’s alopecia was sometimes interpreted as retribution for sins, including adultery.

senses.d: On a certain occasion in the past; once.
ex: For yee were sometimes darkenesse, but now are yee light in the Lord: walke as children of light […]

senses.d: Former; sometime.
ex: Farewell old Gaunt, thy ſometimes brothers wife / With her companion Greefe, muſt end her life.
